Abstract
Adolescent suicidal ideation is a critical public health issue, yet empirical evidence on its prevalence and associated factors among adolescents in northern Bangladesh remains limited. This study estimated the 12-month prevalence of suicidal ideation and examined its associated factors among school-going adolescents in Nilphamari District, Bangladesh. A cross-sectional survey was conducted between May and June 2026 among 365 adolescents aged 13–19 years across eight secondary schools and colleges. Self-administered questionnaires assessed suicidal ideation alongside validated tools for depression (PHQ-9), anxiety (GAD-7), and perceived social support (MSPSS). Factors associated with suicidal ideation were examined using multivariable logistic regression. The 12-month prevalence of suicidal ideation was 30.7% (112/365; 95% CI 26.0%–35.7%). In the primary multivariable model, moderate depression (AOR = 6.05, 95% CI 1.03-35.38; p = 0.046) and moderately severe depression (AOR = 6.86, 95% CI 1.05-44.62; p = 0.044) were associated with higher odds of suicidal ideation compared to minimal depression. However, this association was not statistically significant in a sensitivity analysis using the PHQ-8 score after excluding Item 9 (AOR = 1.06, 95% CI: 0.96-1.17; p = 0.228). Loneliness “often” showed the strongest association with suicidal ideation (AOR = 10.59, 95% CI: 2.53-44.35; p = 0.001). Suicidal ideation was also associated with truancy of 6–9 days (AOR 4.44, 95% CI 1.24–15.90; p = 0.022), truancy of 	≥10 days (AOR 3.77, 95% CI 1.34–10.59; p = 0.012), intentional self-harm (AOR = 2.51, 95% CI: 1.17–5.41; p = 0.018), and physical harm exposure (AOR = 2.63, 95% CI: 1.24–5.57; p = 0.012). Maternal secondary education was associated with lower odds of suicidal ideation (AOR = 0.34, 95% CI: 0.12–0.99; p = 0.048). Suicidal ideation was common among school-going adolescents in northern Bangladesh, affecting nearly one in three participants. Early school-based identification and support for adolescents experiencing mental-health and psychosocial difficulties, together with family engagement and strengthened suicide-prevention services, are warranted.

Physician-scientists are well placed to do translational and clinical research.
Credit: Janiec Bros/Getty
Medical doctors who also do research are an increasingly rare breed. Physician-scientists made up nearly 5% of the US medical workforce in the 1980s; today, that figure is closer to 1.5%
1
. In the United Kingdom, the proportion of senior doctors working as academics fell from almost 5% in 2009 to roughly 3% in 2025 (see ‘Physician-scientists on the ropes’), with the number of physician-scientists under the age of 36 plunging by a whopping 25% between 2024 and 2025 (see
go.nature.com/4ygjfev
). In Japan, 2.1% of all doctors were physician-scientists in 1996; this proportion dropped to 1.6% in 2016. Moreover, the number of physician-scientists aged 39 or younger halved in the same period
2
.

Underlying the decline is an inability to retain young physician-scientists at a high enough rate to replace senior professionals as they retire. Around the world, clinical academics describe funding instability and a lack of career support as barriers to staying in their posts
3
–
6
. In the United States, according to a survey posted on the preprint website medRxiv, more than half of early-career physician-scientists are considering quitting their academic duties to pursue a purely clinical career
7
. That’s
markedly higher
than the 31% of US physicians who report considering leaving their current post within two years.
This trend is alarming because physician-scientists are hugely valuable for health-care research. Their expertise makes them ideally placed to pioneer advances in translational medicine, formulate and run medical trials to improve clinical practice, and drive economic growth. More than one-third of the Nobel Prizes in Physiology or Medicine and Lasker Awards for basic science have been awarded to physician-scientists
8
.
Source:
go.nature.com/4acmbgp
South Korea offers a glimpse of what is at stake. The number of medical research papers it published was already declining — probably owing to funding cuts — when, in 2024, mass resignations by resident physicians forced physician-scientists to abandon research to cover clinical duties
9
. That year, publications fell by 12%, roughly double the decline in the previous year, presumably in part because of the lack of papers from physician-scientists.
Our own experiences have further convinced us of the value of this group. Two of us (R.M. and R.B.) currently lead the University College London MB–PhD programme, which has run since 1994. It enables undergraduate medical students to undertake a PhD in scientific research, typically between their fourth and fifth years — one of several routes to becoming a physician-scientist. Papers authored by our cohort of 131 graduates from the programme between 1994 and 2026 received about three times as many citations each per year as did comparable papers in related fields
10
.
These results are just a snapshot from a small group, and there are many factors that could contribute to the cohort’s high performance. However, we think that they highlight the importance of the blended expertise that defines physician-scientists.
That expertise is now eroding around the world. Governments, funders, universities and others must take urgent steps to stop the decline.
Reasons for the drop-off
In many countries, medical graduates are matched to their first postgraduate positions by centralized, algorithmic systems built for all physicians. A winning video showing beating airway cilia has been disqualified from the Small World in Motion competition for failing to comply with competition rules.
Credit: Ning Xu/Nikon Small World
The winning entry of the prestigious Small World in Motion microscopy competition has been disqualified after scientists raised concerns about its creation using artificial intelligence.
On 9 October, Nikon Instruments, which runs the competition, said
in a statement
that the winning video did not comply with competition rules. AI-generated videos are not permitted, according to the competition website.
The video was submitted by Ning Xu, an optical engineer at the National University of Singapore. It showed the movement of hair-like structures called cilia in the lungs and was awarded first place on 15 September. But in days, scientists noted on social-media platform LinkedIn that some features in the video seemed
biologically implausible
.
In response to those comments, Xu wrote on LinkedIn that his team had used an AI model in post-processing to enhance the visual presentation of the regions below the cilia “without making anatomical claims about what those rendered features represent”. These posts, which appeared under Nikon’s earlier announcement on LinkedIn that Xu had won the prize, have since been taken down.
On 25 September, a Nikon Small World spokesperson told
Nature
that the company was investigating the video. In its latest statement, Nikon Instruments said that after re-evaluating the video and supporting materials, and consulting the judging panel, it determined that the winning video did not comply with the competition rules. “This decision is based solely on the submitted video’s eligibility under the rules outlined for this competition. It should not be interpreted as a judgment of the entrant’s professional reputation, scientific contributions, or intent,” the company said.
Xu did not respond to
Nature
’s request for comment about Nikon’s decision to disqualify his entry. A spokesperson for the National University of Singapore said Ning Xu participated in the competition before he joined the university and the content of his submission is unrelated to his work there.
